title: High throughput method for simultaneous screening of membrane permeability and toxicity for discovery of new cryoprotective agents.
source_license: CC BY-NC-ND as indexed by Europe PMC; raw source retained locally only
study_design: Plate-reader fluorescence quenching screen of 27 candidate CPAs at two temperatures, with sucrose as nonpermeating control; no freeze-thaw efficacy screen.

experiments.model: Bovine pulmonary artery endothelial cells in 96-well plates
experiments.intervention: 27 CPA candidates at approximately 1 molar and 4 degrees C
experiments.comparator: Untreated/reference fluorescence and glycerol permeability benchmark
experiments.outcome_name: Calcein-based short-exposure viability and solute permeability
experiments.timepoint: approximately 25 minutes exposure at 4 degrees C
experiments.result: 23 chemicals met the authors' 80% viability threshold and had permeability at least as high as glycerol. This is a short-exposure property screen, not a demonstration of preserved cell function after freezing.
experiments.sample_size: Minimum 13 permeability replicates and 4 viability replicates per Figure 6A; not independent donors
experiments.source_locator: Results paragraphs Par14 and Par18; Figure 6A caption
experiments.evidence_excerpt: 23 chemicals were nontoxic during short term

experiments.model: Same bovine endothelial cell screening platform
experiments.intervention: 27 CPA candidates at approximately 2 molar and 25 degrees C
experiments.comparator: 80% viability decision threshold; 4-degree screen used different concentration and exposure time
experiments.timepoint: approximately 20 minutes exposure at 25 degrees C
experiments.result: Six chemicals were classified as toxic at 25 degrees C. The 4- versus 25-degree comparison also changes concentration and exposure duration and should not be treated as an isolated causal temperature effect.
experiments.sample_size: Minimum 16 permeability replicates and 4 viability replicates per Figure 6B
experiments.evidence_excerpt: six chemicals were found to be toxic

main_finding: A practical high-throughput filter can identify permeable, low-toxicity candidates before cryopreservation experiments.
limitations: Single bovine endothelial model; short exposure does not establish safety at vitrification concentrations.
Approximately 1 M at 4 degrees C and 2 M at 25 degrees C are not matched exposure conditions.
No post-thaw efficacy, long-term function, or direct ice-inhibition outcome in this screening study.
mechanism_claim: Direct permeability and exposure-toxicity measurements; physical ice protection and cell-death pathway inhibition remain untested.

title: Screening for cryoprotective agent toxicity and toxicity reduction in mixtures at subambient temperatures.
source_license: Abstract metadata; publisher full-text access not acquired
study_design: High-throughput exposure-toxicity screen of 22 individual CPAs and binary mixtures at subambient temperature; abstract-level extraction.

experiments.intervention: 6 mol/kg formamide plus 6 mol/kg glycerol at 4 degrees C

formulation.unit: mol/kg, denominator not specified in abstract
mol/kg, denominator not specified in abstract

experiments.result: Abstract reports 20% viability with formamide alone versus 97% after adding glycerol, increasing total CPA concentration from 6 to 12 mol/kg. This illustrates toxicity neutralization, not a matched-total-concentration post-thaw comparison.

main_finding: Certain mixtures reduced exposure toxicity despite increased total CPA concentration, motivating formulation-level screens.
limitations: Abstract-only evidence: exposure time, assay definition, replication, mixture denominator, and full protocol require full text.
Improved exposure viability does not demonstrate vitrification or post-thaw functional recovery.
The formamide example changes total concentration and cannot isolate an interaction without additional controls.
mechanism_claim: Observed mixture-dependent toxicity reduction; biochemical mechanism and physical cryoprotection are not established by the abstract.

title: Machine learning and hypothesis driven optimization of bull semen cryopreservation media.
study_design: Iterative extender optimization using differential evolution and supervised models, followed by comparison with a commercial/reference extender.
interventions: Gaussian process regression plus differential evolution

experiments.intervention: Generation 21 media optimized using relative total motility
experiments.comparator: Commercial control medium in the same generation
experiments.cooling: 4 hours equilibration at 4 degrees C; 4 to -12 at 4 degrees C/min, -12 to -40 at 40 degrees C/min, -40 to -140 at 50 degrees C/min; plunge into liquid nitrogen
experiments.storage: Liquid nitrogen for at least 24 hours
experiments.result: Generation 21 median motility was 68.3% versus 65.3% for commercial medium; the pooled generation comparison was not statistically different (reported p=0.14). The result supports competitive formulation optimization, not proven superiority to the commercial reference.
experiments.sample_size: Four bulls per generation, eight generated media plus control, triplicate straws; statistical comparison reports m=32 and n=4
experiments.evidence_excerpt: median post-thaw motility for the control medium was 65.3%

experiments.intervention: ANN and Gaussian process models trained on initial measured extender responses
experiments.result: Models used 200 extender-response pairs from generations 1-5 to predict 32 pairs in generation 6. The paper selected GPR based on its representation of experimental variability despite lower ANN prediction error; prospective follow-up gains were less dramatic than the main optimization trials.
experiments.sample_size: 200 training pairs and 32 test pairs; correlated biological data, not 232 independent donors
experiments.evidence_excerpt: Unfortunately, the gains seen in previous trials

main_finding: A measured-data optimization loop produced competitive extenders with far fewer candidates than exhaustive factorial enumeration; superiority did not uniformly persist in follow-up.
limitations: Bull sperm is methods-transfer evidence and does not establish iPSC efficacy.
Multiple observations share bulls and generations; split design matters.
Motility is not an in vivo fertility outcome.
Full Results distinguish generation 17 and 21 metrics; abstract wording should not be substituted for those comparisons.
mechanism_claim: Formulation optimization with biological endpoints; no single molecular mechanism or dual-action CPA established.

title: A highly active mineral-based ice nucleating agent supports in situ cell cryopreservation in a high throughput format.
study_design: Controlled versus uncontrolled extracellular ice nucleation in 96-well plates, with infrared thermography and immediate or delayed neutral-red cell recovery assays.
interventions: LDH1 potassium feldspar in IceStart arrays

experiments.model: HepG2 monolayers in 100 microliter freezing medium per well
experiments.comparator: Uncontrolled nucleation; manual nucleation as an additional positive control
experiments.cooling: 1 degree C/min from +4 to -80 degrees C
experiments.warming: 20 minutes at -20 degrees C, then 37-degree blocks with warm medium; melting typically within 2 minutes
experiments.outcome_name: Neutral-red viable cell recovery normalized to nonfrozen reference
experiments.timepoint: Immediate post-thaw assessment; dye uptake assay includes 2-hour equilibration
experiments.result: Overall recovery was 46.2% with IceStart, 45.3% with manual nucleation, and 16.6% with uncontrolled nucleation. Controlled methods improved recovery; IceStart was not significantly different from manual nucleation.
experiments.sample_size: Eight replicate plates in the immediate assessment
experiments.source_locator: Results, high-throughput cell cryopreservation; Figure 7; cell freezing and viability methods

experiments.model: HepG2 monolayers after extended recovery culture
experiments.cooling: 1 degree C/min from +4 to -80 degrees C
experiments.warming: -20-degree prewarming hold then warm blocks and medium
experiments.outcome_name: Neutral-red viable cell number normalized to matched nonfrozen culture
experiments.result: Overall normalized recovery averaged 80.5% with IceStart versus 53.1% with uncontrolled nucleation. This delayed measure incorporates attachment, survival, and proliferation; it is not an initial-cell survival fraction.
experiments.sample_size: Eight replicate plates in the 5-day assessment
experiments.source_locator: Results, Figure 7 and Figure 8; neutral-red assay methods

main_finding: Controlling extracellular ice nucleation improved recoverable HepG2 monolayers; suppressing every form of ice is not the right target for all protocols.
limitations: Single transformed hepatic cell line; no iPSC generalization.
Neutral-red recovery is not a cell-specific potency assay.
Delayed normalized counts include growth.
Nucleator delivery, temperature gradients, and plate geometry are integral to the result.
mechanism_claim: Nucleation temperature and recovery were measured; downstream intracellular-ice and mechanical explanations are partly mechanistic interpretation.

title: Proline pre-conditioning of cell monolayers increases post-thaw recovery and viability by distinct mechanisms to other osmolytes.
study_design: Osmolyte preconditioning, factorial PVA supplementation, physical ice assays, recovery/growth measurements, and proteomic follow-up.

experiments.intervention: 24-hour proline preincubation followed by DMSO freezing, with or without PVA

formulation.unit: mg/mL; representative value within reported 2-5 mg/mL beneficial range

experiments.cooling: Freezing solution removed; CoolCell plate at 1 degree C/min to -80 degrees C
experiments.warming: 500 microliters complete medium warmed to 37 degrees C added rapidly
experiments.outcome_name: Trypan-blue viable attached-cell recovery relative to prefreeze count
experiments.result: DMSO alone yielded below 25% recovery; proline preconditioning increased recovery to approximately 50%, and adding 2-5 mg/mL PVA increased it to approximately 60%. PVA without preconditioning had no significant positive effect. Nonattached cells were excluded and the 24-hour measure can include growth.
experiments.source_locator: Results and discussion, paragraphs around Figure 2; cryopreservation methods

experiments.model: Cell-free osmolyte solutions and A549 preconditioning model
experiments.intervention: Proline, betaine, and alanine compared with PVA and DMSO controls
experiments.comparator: PBS and 5 mg/mL PVA physical assay controls; standard culture biological controls
experiments.outcome_name: Splat IRI assay and DSC; contextual proteomic interpretation
experiments.timepoint: Splat assay annealing for 30 minutes at -8 degrees C
experiments.result: The osmolytes were not considered IRI-active under the tested conditions; DSC and ice-growth results supported a biochemical preconditioning explanation. Proteomics did not identify a single causal molecular target. The combination is multi-component protection, not proof of a dual-action proline molecule.
experiments.source_locator: Results and discussion, Figure 1 and Table 1; Conclusions
experiments.evidence_excerpt: the osmolytes alone would not be considered IRI active

main_finding: Biological preconditioning and a physical ice inhibitor had complementary effects in A549 monolayers; cell-type differences and recovery denominator matter.
limitations: Proline dose is shown graphically but not transcribed here; this summary cannot serve as a complete executable protocol.
A549 is a transformed cell line; smaller responses occurred in other tested lines.
Recovery excludes detached cells and includes 24 hours for potential growth.
No single molecular target or direct death-pathway inhibition established.
mechanism_claim: Physical assays argue against proline IRI as the explanation; biological preconditioning is supported but not assigned to a single causal pathway.

title: Direct Measurement of Water States in Cryopreserved Cells Reveals Tolerance toward Ice Crystallization.
source_license: CC BY-NC-ND as indexed by Europe PMC; raw source retained locally only
study_design: Cryo-electron imaging, diffraction and controlled thermal excursions correlated with survival under different CPA mixtures.

experiments.model: HeLa cells on electron microscopy grids
experiments.intervention: DE cryoprotection followed by controlled warming excursions

formulation.unit: %, basis not stated in extracted methods
%, basis not stated in extracted methods

experiments.cooling: Grid plunge freezing in liquid ethane at -170 degrees C
experiments.warming: Controlled subzero excursions then survival assessment; thermal histories varied
experiments.outcome_name: Cryo-EM intracellular ice size correlated with cell survival
experiments.timepoint: After specified thermal excursions and final warming; survival assay timing not extracted
experiments.result: Cells in DE survived intracellular crystals averaging 1-3 micrometers, whereas 0.4-0.8 micrometer crystals were lethal in EAFS. Crystal size tolerance was formulation-dependent; these observations do not establish universal tolerance of intracellular ice.
experiments.source_locator: Results, final paragraph before Discussion; Figure S3
experiments.evidence_excerpt: The tolerable crystal sizes depend specifically on the chosen cryoprotective medium.

main_finding: The relationship between ice, warming and viability depends on formulation; absence of detectable ice is not an adequate universal efficacy surrogate.
limitations: Specialized HeLa cryo-imaging preparation and thermal histories do not directly transfer to iPSC banking.
This extraction does not capture a complete survival assay protocol or biological replicate count.
Observed survival does not demonstrate retained differentiation, genomic integrity, or long-term function.
mechanism_claim: Direct physical measurements are linked to survival, suggesting formulation-dependent ice tolerance rather than only ice elimination.

title: The dominance of warming rate over cooling rate in the survival of mouse oocytes subjected to a vitrification procedure.
source_license: Abstract metadata; full-text API retrieval unsuccessful
study_design: Factorial cooling and warming rate comparison in an ethylene glycol-acetamide-Ficoll-sucrose vitrification solution; abstract-level extraction.

experiments.intervention: Highest warming rate of 2950 degrees C/min
experiments.comparator: Lowest warming rate of 139 degrees C/min across cooling rates
experiments.cooling: 37-1827 degrees C/min measured between +20 and -120 degrees C, cooled to -196 degrees C
experiments.warming: 139-2950 degrees C/min measured between -70 and -35 degrees C
experiments.result: At the fastest warming rate, survival exceeded 80% across cooling rates of 187-1827 degrees C/min. At the slowest warming rate, survival was near zero regardless of cooling rate. The authors interpret slow-warming injury in terms of recrystallization.
experiments.evidence_excerpt: survivals were near 0% regardless of the cooling rate

main_finding: Warming rate can dominate survival in a defined vitrification context and must be recorded in comparative CPA studies.
limitations: Abstract-only; concentration, sample size and assay timing unresolved.
Mouse oocytes differ from iPSCs in geometry, permeability and function.
The proposed ice mechanism should not be treated as directly proven by viability alone.
mechanism_claim: Thermal-rate effect directly tested; intracellular recrystallization explanation is an author interpretation in the abstract.

title: Survival of mouse oocytes after being cooled in a vitrification solution to -196°C at 95° to 70,000°C/min and warmed at 610° to 118,000°C/min: A new paradigm for cryopreservation by vitrification.
source_license: PMC archived author manuscript; check article license before redistribution
study_design: Four cooling rates crossed with five warming rates; extension of the same research group's thermal-rate work, not independent cross-laboratory replication.

experiments.model: Mouse oocytes in a vitrification solution
experiments.intervention: Warming at 118000 degrees C/min after four cooling rates
experiments.comparator: Warming at 610 degrees C/min after the same cooling-rate range
experiments.storage: Cooled to −196 °C in liquid nitrogen; duration not extracted
experiments.timepoint: Morphology and osmotic responsiveness including 2 hours in M16 medium
experiments.result: At 118000 degrees C/min warming, survival was 70-85% regardless of prior cooling rate. At 610 degrees C/min, survival fell from 25% to 0% as cooling rate increased from approximately 95 to 69000 degrees C/min. Faster cooling alone did not ensure survival.
experiments.sample_size: 20 thermal combinations; usually 4–6 replicate runs with about 6 oocytes per Cryotop
experiments.source_locator: Materials and Methods; Assessment of viability; Results; Table 3
experiments.evidence_excerpt: The ability to manifest these characteristics after two hours in M16 is considered a rather stringent test of viability.

main_finding: A wider thermal-rate study reinforces the need to optimize warming jointly with formulation and cooling.
limitations: Mouse oocytes and a vitrification solution; transfer to iPSC systems is not established.
Survival is a morphology/osmotic-response endpoint after 2 h culture, not long-term developmental function.
The mechanistic explanation includes an alternative possibility and is not direct intracellular ice imaging.
Related to the 2009 study by the same group; not independent laboratory replication.
mechanism_claim: Thermal-rate effects are directly compared; recrystallization and devitrification remain alternative mechanistic interpretations.
reviewer: root; Luna methods extraction checked against primary full HTML
